baseline:
A
Pi is fundamentally associated with circles, so its appearance in a system of linear collisions with no apparent curves or rotation is counter-intuitive and surprising.

B
The Conservation of Momentum is the fundamental principle stating that the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant in the absence of external forces.

B
This describes the classic physics problem popularized by 3Blue1Brown. In a frictionless, one-dimensional system with perfectly elastic collisions, a small block is placed between a wall and a much larger block. When the large block is set in motion, the total number of collisions that occur (block-on-block and block-on-wall) corresponds to the digits of pi, with the precision depending on the ratio of the masses.

A
In this classic physics problem, if the ratio of the large mass to the small mass (M/m) is set to a power of 100, such as 100^N, the total number of collisions that occur is equal to the first N+1 digits of Pi. For example, if M/m = 100, there are 31 collisions. If M/m = 10,000, there are 314 collisions.

C
The state of the system (velocities of the two blocks) can be plotted on a 2D graph. Due to the conservation of energy, all possible states lie on the arc of a circle. Each collision moves the point along this arc, and the total number of collisions is determined by the arc's length, which is related to Pi.
